Allocation of Kerosene to NE States 
*1. SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the per capita availability and consumption of kerosene in the 
North-Eastern States, State-wise ws-a-wsthe national average; and 
(b) the details of the steps taken or proposed to be taken by 
Government to increase the allocation of kerosene to North-Eastern States? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) For the year 2002-2003, per capita allocation for distribution under Public 
Distribution System in North-Eastern States is as under:—  
States Per Capita Allocation 
 (Litres/annum) 
Arunachal Pradesh 11.5 
Assam 12.6 
Manipur 11.2 
Meghalaya 11.5 
Mizoram 9.7 
Nagaland 8.6 
Tripura 12.7 
The national average for the year 2002-2003 is 12 litres per annum. 
(b) At present, there is no proposal to increase the allocation of 
kerosene to North-Eastern States. 
SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Madam, I would like to thank 
the hon. Minister for giving information about the per capita availability and 
consumption of kerosene in the North-Eastern States. But, from the reply, it is 
clear that out of seven States, five States, namely, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, 
Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland, have been allotted

SHRI RAM NAIK: Madam, basically, this aspect was decided in a 
traditional way, long ago. So, depending upon various circumstances, it was

SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Madam, I do not agree with

information that kerosene, which is very much needed in remote places, is 
being sold in black market by the black marketeers.

concerned, I do agree that these things do happen. But basically it is a subject 
wherein the State Government has to be active and do that work, because 
public distribution is under the State Government. We also

Bifurcation of UTI 
*2. SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: †  
   SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Unit Trust of India (UTI) has been split into two parts 
namely UTI-I and UTI-II; 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by  Shri V.V. 
Raghavan. 
5 

RAJYA  SABHA [18 February, 2003] 
(b) if so, the details and functions of each of them; and 
(c) what is the purpose of splitting it into two parts? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is placed on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Under the provisions of the Unit Trust of India (Transfer of 
Undertaking and Repeal) Act, 2002, the erstwhile Unit Trust of India has 
been bifurcated, with effect from 1 st February, 2003, into (a) the "specified 
undertaking" viz. UTI-I, comprising of schemes mentioned in Schedule—I 
of the above Act and managed by Government appointed Administrator, 
and (b) the "specified company" viz. UTI-II, comprising of NAV based 
schemes mentioned in Schedule—II of the above Act. 
(c) Government decided to bifurcate UTI to ring fence the liabilities 
on Government with regard to US-64 and assured return schemes of UTI; 
and to distance itself from the mutual fund activities of UTI which are 
regulated by SEBI. 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: Madam, the JPC has pointed out some 
serious charges on the part of the SEBI, RBI and the Ministry of Finance in 
connection with the erstwhile UTI's stock market dealings. May I know from 
the hon. Minister what steps are being taken to book the culprits, in 
accordance with the JPC Report? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: So far as taking action against the officials 
who have been found guilty of misdemeanour or misconduct, as the hon. 
Member knows, it is something that preceded the JPC's establishment. Action 
was taken against the officials; enquiry was ordered, and post enquiry, the 
matter has been referred to a Committee to look into what further action is to 
be taken against each of the officials. I can assure the hon. Member, without 
getting involved in the legalistic minutiae of what would be done or not, that 
those who have been found guilty of misconduct and are established as guilty 
of misconduct, will not be'spared; no one will be spared in that regard. 
 
6

[18 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: Madam, there was a report that the 
Government has given a massive amount of Rs. 14,500 crores in order to bail 
out the erstwhile UTI. What is the justification for putting such a burden on 
the exchequer, which was created by the scam? Would the hon. Minister 
explain it? The amount can be recovered from the culprits themselves. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, if I followed the question, what the 
hon. Member says is that he has, from somewhere, gathered the information 
that Rs. 14,000 plus crores have been paid by the Government, as he 
colourfully put it, to bail out the Unit Trust. I have shared every fact and 
information in this regard with the House when the Bill was enacted by the 
two Houses of Parliament. At that time, the figures were shared with the 
Members of the House. Let me again inform the hon. Member that so far as 
the money that has been paid, the funds given for Unit-64, is concerned, in 
2001 -02, it was Rs. 300 crores and for 2002-03, it was Rs. 938 crores, which 
makes a total of Rs. 1238 crores. On the assured return scheme, cash is nil, 
guarantees of Rs. 1000 crores and bonds worth Rs. 1118 crores. All this is for 
2002-03. A comfort letter has been provided to the Unit Trust to borrow from 
the banks and the comfort letter is of Rs. 450 crores. I have also some 
additional information. A Press release has also gone from the Department of 
Economic Affairs. No doubt, the hon. Member is aware of it. When I said that 
the Government shall honour the redemption scheme and we stand by our 
commitment to it, as this has been approved by the Cabinet. The liability on 
this account as currently calculated, because if we are required to fully 
redeem it, then it will be around Rs. 6000 crores. Now this is all the 
information that I can possibly share. It will be incorrect, therefore, to say that 
something like Rs. 14,000 crores has been paid out. That is an incorrect 
presumption. 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: Madam Deputy Chairman, in the reply the 
reason for bifurcation of the UTI is stated to be 'to ring fence the liabilities on 
Government with regard to US-64 and assured return schemes of UTI.' What 
does it mean? Suppose, the UTI-I a nd the UTI-II finally again land in 
difficulty either due to mismanagement or due to some steps taken by the 
officials, then in that case, does the Government think that the Government 
will not be responsible for the amounts that have been deposited by the 
depositors? In the beginning when the UTI was set up, this was the assurance 
given that this is an organisation sponsored by 
 
7

RAJYA  SABHA [18 February, 2003] 
the Government of India. With that confidence in view, people have invested their 
money. What will be their fate if any such thing happens? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam Deputy Chairman, we have 
examined in great detail this very aspect and the Bill was enacted. I shared 
with the hon. Members then that the bifurcation is, in fact, to fencing the 
liability of the Government and the fencing in of Unit-I from Unit-ll. Let me 
very briefly explain the fundamental of it. Unit-I is Unit-64, the assured 
returned scheme and the special SUS, which was created with the public 
sector companies. The US-64 and the assured return scheme, the Government 
fully stands by. We have committed that we will honour it. In the month of June, 
the redemption will start. There is no question of the Government going back 
on that part of it. And the redemption scheme was announced long back. What 
we have done is to fence in Unit-64, the assured return scheme and SUS from 
Unit-ll. Unit-ll is a net asset value based mutual fund. This Mutual Fund, 
hereafter, governed by the SEBI Regulations is a Mutual Fund that will operate 
like any other Mutual Fund operates in the market. The question of 
mismanagement and, therefore, the Government withdrawing from it, etc., simply 
does not arise when it comes to UNIT-64. As far as UN IT-11 is concerned, it 
is a NAV-based Scheme. It is a Mutual Fund, SEBI regulated, market-controlled 
and this Scheme will, now, be governed, entirely, like any other Mutual Fund 
in the country.

SHRIJAGMOHAN: Madam, there are two parts of the question. One is 
the turndown. Everybody knows that after the September 11 incident, there 
was a downfall in the tourism all over the world. But after October, we have 
now changed the trend. In October, as compared to last October, there has 
been an increase of 16.8 per cent. Similarly, as compared to last November, 
there has been an increase of 16.2 per cent, and, then again, there has been 
another increase. In the month of January, as compared to the month of 
January of last year, the increase is about 22 per cent. So, in terms of number 
as well as in terms of earnings, there is now an upward trend. 
As regards the question why, during the last ten or fifteen years, the 
share of India in the world tourism ha s remained as low as .39 per cent, I 
think, the previous Governments had to answer that, but we are doing our best 
to now increase the tempo of tourism, and I am quite confident that with the 
new measures that we have taken, the setting up of all cultural-cum-tourism 
hubs and six tourism circuits all over the country—at least one in every big 
State is being done and the results are very obvious—there has been a 
tremendous increase in the domestic tourism. There was an increase of about 
24 per cent, in one year, in the domestic tourism. So, there has been an 
upward trend. The hon. Member has mentioned about China. Undoubtedly, 
China has made a tremendous increase. In this respect, we all have to 
understand why China has increased its tourism. One of the main reasons is 
that it is a highly disciplined society. But in our case, we must admit that all 
our tourist monuments are not kept clean; all types of slums, all types of 
stalls, all types of things come around, and whenever any action is taken, 
there is a problem. Everybody knows that. That is why, I think, under the new 
policy, we are emphasizing—and during the last one year, our measures have 
shown the results—that in almost all the areas we have taken special care of 
cleanliness. Ultimately, tourism is a civilisational issue; it all depends upon 
our value system, how we treat the people. How the taxJwallahs cheat the 
tourists, how the policemen cheat the people, how the customs men cheat the 
people, we are trying to look into all those aspects, and, I am sure, we will be 
able to show better results than the ones that have been there before.

Effect of Iraqi war on economy 
19. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any assessment of the likely 
effects of a possible war in Iraq on the Indian economy; and 
(b) if so, what are the main findings thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) 
and (b) The impact of possible war in Iraq on Indian economy will depend 
critically on the duration of conflict. Assuming a short and swift course, with 
a decisive US victory, the major impact would be on international crude oil 
prices, where in the country is well equipped to finance higher import bill in 
the event of a steep escalation of global oil prices or other exogenous 
developments. While there may be a temporary set back to our exports of 
goods and services to the gulf region, overall exports are unlikely to be 
affected too long. Remittances from the gulf region may also go down 
temporarily, the decline being preceded by a probable increase in remittances 
in anticipation of the conflict. With an observed tendency for a surplus in 
current account and comfortable foreign exchange reserves at more than $ 70 
billion, vulnerability of balance of payments to such changes, however, 
appears to be limited in the short run. 
Considering the current inflation rate and level of foodstocks, the 
impact on domestic inflation will be temporary, with hike in oil prices 
unlikely to result in any sharp surge in domestic inflation, Capital 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [18 February, 2003] 
markets may witness a slight stiffening of  interest rates, with limited decline 
in sentiments in stock markets followed by a quick recovery. Depending on 
market sentiments, the rupee may come under pressure, with such 
depreciation of the rupee, coupled with impact of oil price hike on domestic 
inflation, impinging on the current soft interest rate regime. 
Overall, the impact of possible war in Iraq on growth prospects of 
Indian economy is likely to be marginal in the short run. Notwithstanding 
such marginal impact on the economy, the overall growth performance of the 
Indian economy is unlikely to be seriously affected by the developments in 
the Gulf, due to clear signs of revival of domestic demand and the resultant 
buoyancy imparted to the domestic economy.

64. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of

(c) whether Government propose to enact a Legislation for the 
protection and maintenance of ground waters; if so, the details in this regard? 
126 

[18 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) The long-term 
observations made by the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) have shown 
a situation of fall in the level of ground water in various parts of the country. 
The names of the States/districts having pockets with fall in water level in the 
last twenty years (1982-2001) are given in the Statement enclosed. (See 
below). 
(b) Water being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility 
of the concerned State Governments to plan, finance and execute 
schemes for augmenting water resources. The Central Government 
has initiated following measures to  recharge the underground water 
source:— 
(i)    Implementation of a Central Sector Scheme for Study of Recharge 
to Ground Water in the country. 
(ii) Circulation of Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground 
Water to the States/Union Territories to enable them to formulate 
area specific artificial recharge schemes to check the declining 
trend in ground water levels. 
(iii) Organisation of mass awareness programmes and training courses on 
rain water harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. 
(iv) Constitution of Central Ground Water Authority under the 
Environment (Protection) Act 1986  for regulation and control of 
ground water management and development. 
(c) Water being a State subject, suitable legislation for 
regulation and control of ground water development has to be 
enacted by the States/Union Territories. However, the Union 
Government has circulated a Model Bill to regulate and control the 
development of ground water in 1970, which was recirculated in 
1992 and again in 1996 to all the States/Union Territories for 
adoption.

of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state:

of 4 tmc. ft. of water from the Tungabhadra Dam; 
(b) if so, whether the water was meant to meet the drinking 
water requirements of Kurnool city and Adoni and Yemmiganur 
Municipalities in Kurnool district; 
(c) whether there is no response from the officials in Karnataka despite 
repeated pleas for the release of water; and 
(d) if so, whether the Central Gove rnment have agreed to issue 
instructions to Karnataka to release water to Andhra Pradesh? 
134 

[18 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) During 
the month of April, 2002 the demand of Andhra Pradesh for meeting drinking 
water needs of Kurnool Town and other villages could not be meet due to over 
drawal by Karnataka, which has resulted in insufficient storage in Tungabhadra 
reservoir. The matter was deliberated in an emergency meeting of 
Tungabhadra Board held on 6th April, 2002 and it was decided that 
Government of Karnataka would ensure replenishment of excess quantity of 
water drawn from Tungabhadra reservoir in order to meet the immediate 
drinking water requirement of Andhra Pradesh. Accordingly, Karnataka 
Government released water from the reservoirs upstream of the Tungabhadra 
Dam and there was improvement in the inflows into the Tungabhadra 
Reservoir. Thereafter on 29th April, 2002 water could be released from 
Tungabhadra Reservoir to Andhra Pradesh to meet the drinking water needs of 
Kurnool Town and other villages.

Implementation of Dastur Plan 
†101. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are considering to link all 
rivers of the country; 
(b) if so, the details of roadmap thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Government are considering to 
implement 'Dastur Plan' of the decae of sixties; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) The 
Ministry of Water Resources, then known as the Minist ry of Irrigation, 
formulated a National Perspective Plan for water resources development in 
1980 which envisages inter linkages among peninsular rivers and Himalayan 
Rivers for transferring wa ter from water surplus basins  to water deficit areas 
for optimum utilization of water re sources. The Government of India 
established the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) in 1982 as an 
autonomous society to carryout water balance and other studies and prepare 
feasibility reports. NWDA has identified 30 links under the National 
Perspective for preparation of the feasibility reports and has completed 
feasibility reports of 6 links under Peninsular Component. Central 
Government has set up a Task Force on 13.12.2002 to devise suitable 
mechanism to suggest modalities for arriving at consensus amongst the States 
for sharing and transfer of surplus water to deficit area and also to identify the 
priority links which could be implemented quickly as well as mechanism for 
their clearance funding etc. 
(c) and (d) The proposal of Captain Dastur was earlier examined by two 
committees of experts comprising experts from Central Water Commission, 
State Governments and Professors from Indian Institute of Technology and 
University of Roorkee who were of the opinion that the proposal was 
technically unsound and economically prohibitive. The scheme was therefore, 
given up.

Orissa, particularly in Kalahandi, Bolangir and Koraput region - infamous as

persons from outside are manipulating to smuggle out minor girls to other 
parts of India for making money from human misery. While a few instances of 
such deals come to light, majority of cases are never known. During 1994-

remaining hundreds remained untraced. Most of the victims belong to remote 
rural areas whose parents are too backward, besides being too poor, to try to 
recover their lost children. These children are perhaps sold for slavery purpose 
by inhuman locals to known agents from outside who are capable of deporting 
them to other States or even other countries.   It is also possible for merchants

preventing abominable practices. Many measures can be thought of by the

more than one occasion the four procedures which have been adopted to 
value a company. But, from time to time, certain aberrations, certain 
distortions, certain incidents take place, and this unease again crops up, which 
is reinforced. The third cause of unease, which I think, is one of the most 
important cause is the strategic sector. It has been defined, from time to time, 
re-defined, re-redefined and again defined. So, today, when we are dealing 
with the energy sector, is the energy sector a strategic sector or not? The 
original principle of disinvestment was that the Government tias no business to 
be in business, except in the strategic sector. Now, Defence is a strategic 
sector; nuclear energy is a strategic sector, Railways are a strategic sector; is 
energy a strategic sector or not? If so, why are we carrying out disinvestment 
in a strategic sector? These are the causes of unease, which is, I think, the 
reason why this debate keeps recurring from time to time on various 
occasions, whenever various companies come up for disinvestment. As I said, 
disinvestment is based on the principle, 'it is not the Government's 
194 

[18 February. 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
business to be in business.' I think, the origin of this statement is outside this 
country, under an economic environment, which does not perhaps apply to 
this country; because, at this point in time in the 21 s' century, when we are 
attempting to put into practice this principle, 'it is not the business of the 
Government to be in business', I do not think we are taking account of the fact 
that this is being put into effect in an environment where a substantial public 
sector already exists, and therefore, I think to follow a principle, which really 
does not apply one hundred per cent to our environment, is creating this lack 
of cohesion, lack of consensus and general unease in the country. Are we 
going in the right direction? It is not a question of public sector versus private 
sector. As consumers, what we want is product, what we want is efficiency, 
and I must say that those of us - I think all of us -- who have been exposed to 
the public sector in the days of its monopoly, at least in the service sector -- 
banks, airlines -- have realised that it was an extremely inefficient 
organization, at least to the user. Now, perhaps under the pressure of 
competition, perhaps under the threat of privatization, I do see that the public 
sector in the service areas has certainly improved a lot. So, perhaps there is 
something to it. I think the Government may like to consider adopting, as some 
of us have been saying, a via-media model, an Indian model which has been 
mooted by various sources from time to time, that is, those public sector 
companies which are in the strategic sector; and we must now lay down 
definitely what the strategic sector is. These should be managed by a holding 
corporation. This idea has been mooted in several instances. The Government 
could perhaps consider setting up a holding corporation in which the modality 
would be -- you privatize the management, but do not privatise the company; 
and let the profits which are coming from the profit-making PSUs in the 
strategic sector continue flowing into the Government, but divest the 
Government of direct responsibility for the day-to-day overseeing of 
commercial operations. Let this be a holding, something on the lines of 
financial restructuring being carried out in other areas like UTI etc., and let this 
sense of unease be removed. Let us get the benefits of a well-run public 
sector in the strategic areas, and as far as the non-strategic areas are 
concerned, we can then consider seriously privatization of the non-strategic 
areas, provided our other concerns of valuation and utilization of proceeds are 
met to the satisfaction of the Parliament.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY): Mr.

SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, last 
year, in the month of December, this House had a detailed discussion 
regarding disinvestment of both these oil companies. HPCL and BPCL. The 
Hon. Minister has given the reply to this House. But the Minister was not able 
to justify the reason for the disinvestment of the two companies, and still the 
cloud of doubt remains. Who is the real beneficiary from the disinvestment of 
these two companies? Whether the Government is able to convince the people 
of this country that by way of disinvesting these two oil companies, HPCL and 
BPCL, the Government or the people are going to be benefited by way of 
disinvestment. So, my first question to the Minister is: Who is the real 
beneficiary of this disinvestment process? It is being said that the proceeds of 
the disinvestment will be utilised in the social sector. As far as social 
commitment of this Government is concerned, suppose this Government is not 
convinced or not committed to the cause of the people, the cause of the 
working class, who are working in these public sector companies -- how can 
this Government fulfil the ambitions, or, fulfil the aims of the public at large in 
this country? So, the disinvestment is only to help the corporate houses. There 
is no doubt about that. We know what the corporate houses or the private 
companies are doing in this country. As far as NPA is concerned, it has 
crossed Rs. One lakh crores. Evasion of tax and so many other things are 
there. These two public sector companies are paying huge dividends. They are 
paying all legal dues to the Government. The exchequer is benefited by these 
two public sector companies. If these national assets are sold to the private 
corporate houses, from where will the wealth come in future? What is the 
apprehension of the Government and the Minister? They are giving an 
explanation that in future these companies will not be able to face competition 
and they will not be globally competitive. The statistics have come before the 
House. I am not going into the statistics because of lack of time. It is very well 
known that these two pioneer nava ratna companies are able to compete in 
the global scenario.    Then, why should they be
